bet.text: One familiar telescoping arm, based on the 2023 robot's, does all the major game tasks and also pulls the robot up the cage.

demand.text: Must-have targets: drive, deep cage climb, coral on L1 to L4 from the ground, station and mark, and algae from floor and reef into the net. The team wanted to be able to play any alliance role, put playoff and Einstein-level play first, and decided very early that the highest levels needed a fast, consistent climb.

auto.text: A commentator on the district championship finals describes an auto that goes all the way around the reef for L4, L4, L3 and L3, leaving partners free to run normal autos of their own.
Another says it ran lollipop autos on Einstein.
The front-face auto starts against the wall and scores only that face, to suit partners running station autos.

cycle.text: The intake collects and orients coral. The driver picks level and left or right; the robot picks the reef face, front or back scoring and which camera to trust, drives in, moves the arm and ejects once in tolerance.
1690's account says it went for their lollipop algae in Einstein finals 2 and took a dropped one in finals 3.

endgame.text: Wheels pull one bar of the deep cage into one-way latches, and wheel speed and current show possession. The arm pulls down and locks into the bumper frame while a carriage keeps the chain above the center of gravity. The team states a 1.5-second climb.

fallback.text: Rotation-based reef selection picks the face from the gyro and the tags in view instead of from odometry.
It suits plans with much field travel, when wheel odometry may have slipped.

gave_up.text: The team chose to ignore its 'Aggressively Simple' and 'Lightweight' objectives. Its no-effort list includes the shallow climb, buddy climbs, taking coral off the reef and controlling coral and algae at once.
The arm can be time-consuming to repair.
With only one full robot, coming apart for checked luggage became a design constraint.

changed.text: The intake went through V1 (never competed), V2 at Sammamish, V2.2 at Auburn and V3 at the district championship and Worlds.
The wrist moved from belt to chain after skipping teeth, and the 2023 arm's extension belt, which had been overloaded, became chain.
MK4i modules gave way to prototype MK5 at Worlds; the weight saved went into a second brass bar.

outcome.text: 66-7-0 in official play; won the Newton division, won the championship; pick 1 of the Newton alliance on Einstein; ranked 2 of the pooled top 20 (OPR 127.87, Newton).

solves.text: Short cycles, and surviving a season of high-speed collisions

facts.text: 2 x 1 in chassis with SDS lowering kits to lower the center of gravity
MK4i modules with L2 gearing and eight Kraken X60 through the district championship
Prototype MK5 modules at Worlds: four X60 drive, four X44 steer, enclosed gears, 2.25 in wide wheels
The MK5 change saved about this much, spent on another brass bar in the rear frame
The PDP feeds 20 motors; the other four slots feed the radio, the roboRIO, the Limelights, and everything else
A flexible TPU mount isolates the roboRIO from shock and covers the case seam, after the 2024 unit was found full of carpet fuzz

functions.name: Brass ballast

solves.text: Move the center of mass forward and counteract the arm's motion

functions.type: solid brass bar at the front of the chassis

facts.text: Bar weight
The battery sits at the front too, for easy access and a low center of gravity
Weight of the insert added in the rear frame rail before the championship; with MK4i modules the robot would have been overweight
The middle front bumper has a steel backing plate as more ballast, and sits lower to clear the wrist chains

functions.name: Pivot

solves.text: Make the pivot robust and stiff, with the gearboxes low in the drivebase

functions.type: dead-axle arm pivot on an A-frame

facts.text: Three Kraken X60 with a #35 chain final reduction
Gear ratio
A cradle softens impacts and gives a hard stop for zeroing
A kickstand holds the arm in the starting configuration while disabled
The offset pivot allows a stowed pose with a very low center of gravity
Two gear stages then chain, one gear stage fewer than in 2023, to cut backlash; a swing arm tensions the chain
The arm sprocket is held by four 1/4-20 bolts through both arm plates, with no twisting or bending
Calculator estimate, 90 degrees when scoring: 0.32 s at 14 A per motor; when climbing: 0.35 s at 43 A per motor. The robot did not necessarily move this fast
Commanded with Motion Magic; velocity is the only feedforward, and one team post thinks all arm axes share the same PID constants, set at the motor shaft

solves.text: Stop the overloaded extension belt of the 2023 arm from breaking

facts.text: Three Kraken X60 with a #25 chain final reduction
Gear ratio
The extension sprocket is coaxial on the pivot axle, so the motors stay in the base
Stage 1 runs on two #25 chains and stage 2 on 3 mm UHMWPE string
Stage 1 tube is machined from 2.5 in x 3/16 in wall to 2.375 in x 1/8 in wall, and stage 2 from 2 in x 1/8 in to 1.875 in x 1/16 in, to fit the chain inside
Rotating the pivot moves the coaxial extension, so code adds a coupling ratio times the shoulder angle to the extension setpoint
Up-pull and down-pull strings anchor at the bottom of stage 2; each chain loop is in two segments with a tensioner, so it closes outside the assembled arm
Larger string pulleys than in 2023 take real bearings, which cut friction, and a thicker string, after the 2023 string once broke
Calculator estimate for full travel: 0.37 s at 11 A per motor
Tubes with a 1/16 in wall were ruled out for stages 0 and 1 because the end blocks need tapped holes

cost.text: The arm tubes, extension bearing blocks, pivot axle and plugs are the hardest parts to machine
String grew about 3/4 in before it broke in; slack string leaves its pulleys and abrades, so it was retensioned often at first
Rigging an arm takes about an hour and its wiring and cable chain two or more
Harder to manufacture than the 2023 arm, in exchange for robustness and service; bearing blocks like these took six setups on a 3-axis mill
The igus 045-20-018 cable chain broke twice in practice from impacts, never at a competition

solves.text: Score forwards or backwards with one compact, light joint

facts.text: Over 180 degrees of motion from one Kraken X44
Moved to #25 chain after the belt skipped teeth under a heavier, longer intake
Wrist travel, against 192 degrees in 2023; idler sprockets route the chain clear of the arm bearings
The motor rides on the intake plates: a gear stage, then two 12:38 chain stages, the last doubled for strength, ending on sprockets fixed to the arm
One steel rod with a cam at each end tensions all three chains, which share a length

cost.text: Wall hits and lowering onto coral bent the tension rod as a 1/4-20 bolt and as a 3/8 in steel rod; a 1/2 in steel rod held

solves.text: Take coral instantly in any orientation, then turn it for the level

facts.text: Four vertical wheels and a set of horizontal wheels turn coral lengthwise for L2 to L4 or horizontal for L1
Four CANrange sensors detect coral and index it for scoring front, back or sideways
One Kraken X60 on the horizontal rollers, two X44 on the vertical wheels
V3 split the funneling wheels onto two motors and added two CANranges for easy horizontal L1 scoring
2 in solid-core flex wheels held L1 coral much better than the clipped compliant wheels
V3 weight, down from about 15 lb for V1, with smaller, more lightened plates
Before V3, softer wheels on one side than the other let coral hit flat slide over and turn in; V3 drives each side separately, so this was dropped
Floor pickup is lined up by the driver, with no object detection
The vertical rollers were wiped with baby wipes before every match, and new wheels performed better

cost.text: V1 could stall a coral grabbed exactly in the middle, slipped wheels on printed hubs and skipped belts

functions.name: Algae intake

solves.text: Pick algae from the floor and the reef with the coral end effector

functions.type: shared lower wheels plus upper roller

facts.text: The coral intake's horizontal wheels and an upper compliant-wheel roller grab algae
The upper roller was moved back, because in V1 it interfered with coral pickup at a wall
Roller reductions: about 7.1:1 lower, 8.3:1 upper. Holding algae uses a 100 A stator limit, which kept an X60 on the lower roller

cost.text: 3/8 in bore bearings on the algae shafts failed twice in collisions; both times the mechanism worked to the end of the match

functions.name: Climber

solves.text: Climb fast without precise alignment and without a separate lifting subsystem

functions.type: powered grabber with latches, lifted by the arm

facts.text: Two wheels on one Kraken X44 take in a single bar of the cage
Passive spring-loaded latches hold the bar; a lower V wedge gives a reaction point
The arm's extension hooks the front bumper frame to lock it down
Stated climb time
Automated once the bar is in the latches, which wheel speed and current reveal; no trouble from false positives

cost.text: In one Einstein match the bar seems to have rolled out of one side of a latch as the arm pulled down, which the team says very rarely happens

solves.text: Keep the chain above the center of gravity so the robot does not swing and touch the ground

facts.text: One Kraken X60 moves it through a gearbox and #25 chain on the bottom of the arm
It lets the robot grab near the top of the cage and pull down as the arm rotates
With a fixed mount the layout sketches left 0.5 to 1.5 in under the rear bumper at best, before any slip on the cage
Calculator estimate for full travel: 0.57 s at 14 A

functions.name: Automated scoring

solves.text: Leave the driver only the level and the side to choose

functions.type: four Limelight 4 cameras with a state machine

facts.text: Cameras on the pivot structure align to the reef from the front and back
Pose-based mode picks the closest reef face by odometry; rotation-based mode uses the gyro's nearest 60-degree angle and the tags seen
One button pushes a system state to the superstructure, which delegates to subsystems
Odometry is hard reset to camera poses, with no pose estimator, only on reef tags and only while auto-scoring
Alignment uses no motion profile, after trapezoidal profiles and dynamic path following were tried, and adds friction compensation, which helped most when starting close to the goal
Autos and reef alignment drive straight to a point: PID on the straight-line distance, split into X and Y, with a separate clamped heading PID
Choreo splines start some autos: one team post names the four-piece front-face auto, another the mark auto
Distance comes from the tag height in pixels, which camera pitch does not affect; of two solutions the farther is used, since the nearer would be inside the reef
The cameras see the whole tag of the target face through the entire scoring sequence, front or back
L1 stacking has one button for the base layer and one for the top; driving in, release, wait and backing out are automatic
Controller paddles replace the face buttons so thumbs stay on the sticks, and bindings change with the piece held

cost.text: A reply notes the pixel-height method is ambiguous and cannot be reused carelessly, for example with tags high up

solves.text: Replace an arm that is slow to repair with a spare

facts.text: One bolt holds the two end plugs of the pivot axle; removing it frees the whole arm
Pivot, extension, wrist and climber are zeroed against hard stops with one button before the match
Arm swap time, with a complete spare carried to events
Homing can also run in a match: one team post counts two uses at most all season, after heavy impacts; a later one says a few, when an axis skipped teeth
Absolute encoders, planned for the 2023 arm, proved very hard to fit on the dead-axle pivot and reverted wrist, so 2025 again used motor encoders only

decisions.choice: Base the arm on the 2023 robot's
decisions.because: familiarity freed effort for the intake and climber and made assembly and repairs smoother

decisions.choice: Use the arm as the climb's main actuator
decisions.because: a fast, consistent climb was judged necessary, and it is simpler and lighter

decisions.choice: Grip a single bar of the cage with a powered collector
decisions.because: it reduces the need for precise alignment
the 2023 belt was overloaded and broke, and the 2025 arm and intake are heavier

decisions.choice: Zero on hard stops before the match
decisions.because: it removes sensors that might need recalibration when the arm is swapped
the second robots of 2023 and 2024 were late or unfinished, and on the shared practice fields the team is usually limited to one robot at a time
decisions.cost: the robot must come apart to fly as checked luggage

decisions.choice: Two motors on the V3 funneling wheels
decisions.because: it makes horizontal L1 scoring easy and let the front roller be wider
decisions.instead_of: one X60 driving all the funneling wheels on V1

decisions.because: the robot is steadier then, so the poses are accurate enough

decisions.choice: A powered carriage for the climber
decisions.because: just over a week after kickoff the team could not be sure a fixed mount would clear the floor, and adding a carriage later might not have been possible

decisions.choice: A separate motor for the climber carriage
decisions.because: a motor and weight were available, and the full retracted position might not always be wanted
decisions.instead_of: rigging that couples the carriage to arm rotation

decisions.choice: Three motors on both the pivot and the extension
decisions.because: each axis is sized early for 0.25 to 0.5 s and under 20 A per motor, the 2023 extension was motor-limited, and removing a motor is easier than adding one; the team says two on the pivot would certainly work
the team believes 6061 would have bent at the first wall hit, and it avoids polycarbonate for floppiness or cracking
the team had struggled with MegaTag and a pose estimator, and needed a day to work out and add the math

decisions.choice: Net scoring left to the driver
decisions.because: a color sensor for stopping on the floor tape had too much latency, and pose was expected to drift over long algae runs

decisions.choice: Net scoring from the front only, as of early April
decisions.because: scoring over the back had not been tested or ruled out, but the wrist angle would hold algae much lower there, and ejection already used full voltage
features not expected in Einstein playoff matches are devalued

decisions.choice: Score on the front and over the back
decisions.because: the arm turned out to allow both, so front cameras were added
decisions.instead_of: over the back only, as first planned

decisions.because: it has crimped main lugs; main wires had twice come loose from PDH terminals

decisions.choice: Spend motors, weight and strength rather than optimize
decisions.because: time in the season is short, and not redesigning a failed part is worth more
